specPoints.text: determine the distance travelled from the area between a velocity−time graph and the time axis

primer.text: A velocity-time graph hides a second answer beneath its line: the distance covered. This lesson shows why the enclosed area counts metres, gives the two area formulas you need, and then assembles a whole 160-second car journey out of five separate shapes.

lessons.title: What the area under the line counts
sourceHeadings: How to find the area under a velocity-time graph
lessons.opening: Gradient reads one answer off this graph; area reads the other. Between the line and the time axis sits a region whose size is measured in metres, because it multiplies a velocity by a time. This lesson establishes the counting rule and the two area formulas that carry it.
keyPoints: The area between a velocity-time line and the time axis represents the displacement, that is the distance travelled.
A triangular region appears when the object accelerates or decelerates, and its area is one half times the base times the height.
A rectangular region appears when the object moves at constant velocity, and its area is base times height.
The base of each shape is a time interval and the height is a velocity, so the unit of every area is metres.

low.restatement: Shade the space between the line and the horizontal axis. If that space is a rectangle, multiply velocity by time. If it is a triangle, halve the product.
low.analogy: It is like earning money at a steady rate: rate times hours gives total earnings, and the 'total' here is the distance covered.
low.examPointer: Quote the unit: an area read as (10 m/s) × (4 s) is 40 m. An answer of '40' with no unit forfeits the mark.

medium.restatement: The rule works dimensionally: (m/s) × (s) = m, which is why area on this graph is a distance. Triangle versus rectangle is decided by the motion: changing velocity makes a triangle, steady velocity makes a rectangle.
medium.analogy: A rectangle is one steady wage; a triangle is a wage rising linearly from zero, whose total is exactly half the rectangle built on its final rate.
medium.examPointer: Displacement and distance are used interchangeably in this reading when the line stays at or above the axis; say 'distance travelled' in answers.

check.stem: What does the area between a velocity-time line and the time axis represent?

options.text: The distance travelled during that interval
options.explanation: Enclosed area multiplies velocity by time, which is exactly a distance.

options.text: The acceleration gained
options.explanation: Acceleration is the gradient of the line, not the area beneath it.

options.text: The average velocity
options.explanation: Average velocity would be a height, not an area; the area counts metres.

options.text: The time the journey lasted
options.explanation: Time is the base of the shape, already measured along the horizontal axis.

check.stem: The region under a straight rising section is a triangle with base 8 s and height 12 m/s. What distance does it encode?

options.text: 48 m, from one half of 8 × 12
options.explanation: Triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 8 × 12 = 48 m.

options.text: 96 m, from 8 × 12
options.explanation: 96 m is the full rectangle; the triangular half is wanted for a rising section.

options.text: 20 m, from 8 + 12
options.explanation: Areas multiply their sides; adding a time and a velocity has no meaning.
That quotient would be an acceleration, not the distance the area encodes.

check.stem: A section of line sits perfectly flat at 9 m/s for 7 s. What shape is the enclosed region and what distance does it hold?

options.text: A rectangle holding 63 m, from 9 × 7
options.explanation: Constant velocity makes a rectangle: base 7 s times height 9 m/s = 63 m.

options.text: A triangle holding 31.5 m
options.explanation: Triangles belong to changing velocity; a flat section makes a rectangle.

options.text: A rectangle holding 16 m, from 9 + 7
options.explanation: The sides multiply; adding gives neither an area nor a distance.

options.text: No region exists under a flat line
options.explanation: A flat line above the axis encloses the largest rectangle of all: velocity times the whole interval.

check.stem: Why does the area under this graph carry the unit metres rather than any other unit?

options.text: Because the sides multiply metres per second by seconds, and the seconds cancel
options.explanation: (m/s) × (s) leaves m: the unit arithmetic is the whole justification.

options.text: Because areas are always measured in metres
options.explanation: Area units follow the axes: on a distance-time graph the enclosed area would be m·s, not m.

options.text: Because the graph is drawn on squared paper
options.explanation: The paper is irrelevant; the unit comes from the quantities on the two axes.

options.text: Because velocity is defined as distance divided by area
options.explanation: Velocity is distance over time; the area rule follows from multiplying back by time.

check.stem: An object decelerates in a straight line from 20 m/s to rest over 10 s. Which calculation gives the distance it covers while stopping?

options.explanation: A straight fall to rest is a triangle: base 10 s, height 20 m/s, area 100 m.
200 m is the full rectangle; stopping in a straight line fills only half of it.
That quotient is the deceleration in m/s², not a distance.

options.text: 0 m, because the object ends at rest
options.explanation: Ending at rest says nothing about the ground covered; the triangle holds 100 m.

check.stem: State the two area formulas used to read distances from a velocity-time graph and say which motion each matches.
check.modelAnswer: Triangle: area = ½ × base × height, for changing velocity (accelerating or decelerating). Rectangle: area = base × height, for constant velocity.

check.stem: Recall what the height and the base of an enclosed region correspond to on the graph's axes.
check.modelAnswer: The height is a velocity read from the vertical axis and the base is a time interval read from the horizontal axis.

check.stem: Explain why a straight rising section encloses a triangle rather than a rectangle on a velocity-time graph.
check.modelAnswer: A rising straight line starts low and ends high, so the region between it and the axis is a right triangle whose sloping top is the line itself. A rectangle would need the line to stay at one constant height, which is exactly the constant-velocity case instead.

check.stem: A scooter holds 6.0 m/s for 12 s, then rises in a straight line from 6.0 m/s to 14 m/s over 8.0 s. Calculate the distance covered in each section.
check.modelAnswer: Cruise: rectangle 6.0 × 12 = 72 m. Rise: triangle ½ × 8.0 × 14 = 56 m. The scooter covers 72 m then 56 m in the two sections.

lessons.title: Splitting the region and totalling the journey
sourceHeadings: How to find distance from a velocity-time graph
lessons.opening: Real journeys change pace more than once, so the region under the line comes in pieces. This lesson assembles the total distance by dividing the graph into enclosed rectangles and triangles, calculating each, and summing them — the exact routine the 160-second car journey demands.
keyPoints: Constant acceleration keeps the line straight, so the whole region splits into enclosed rectangles and triangles.
Each enclosed section's area is the distance travelled during that section's own time interval.
The total distance is the sum of every individual area under the line.
The worked journey gives areas 350 m, 525 m, 75 m, 350 m and 875 m, summing to 2175 m.
A curved line can be estimated by dividing it into triangles and rectangles the same way.

low.restatement: Chop the space under the line into pieces the axis lines already mark. Work out each triangle and rectangle, then add all the areas together for the whole journey's distance.
low.analogy: It is like adding up a shopping basket item by item: every shape is one cost, and the sum is the bill.
low.examPointer: Label each enclosed area (1, 2, 3…) before calculating; labelled working is what earns method marks when one arithmetic slip lands.

medium.restatement: Interval questions are slicing questions: the distance between two times is exactly the area standing on that slice of the base, however many shapes it takes.
medium.analogy: The total area behaves like a timeline of receipts: any window of time costs exactly what its slice of shapes adds up to.
medium.examPointer: If a slice cuts through a shape, split that shape rather than guessing: the note's areas 3 and 4 are exactly this case.

check.stem: A journey's velocity-time region divides into five enclosed sections. How is the total distance obtained?

options.text: Every area is calculated and the five results are added
options.explanation: Each area is a distance; the journey total is their sum.

options.text: Only the largest section's area matters
options.explanation: Every interval contributes its metres; dropping sections loses part of the journey.

options.text: The five areas are averaged
options.explanation: A mean of areas has no physical meaning; distances accumulate by addition.

options.text: The areas are multiplied together
options.explanation: Multiplying metre-counts together would give m⁵, not a distance.

check.stem: In the worked car journey, one region needs splitting into a triangle and a rectangle. What does that split tell you about the motion in that interval?

options.text: The velocity changed part-way through the interval, first rising then holding
options.explanation: A triangle plus rectangle side by side is the signature of a rise that then flattens within one interval.

options.text: The car reversed direction during the interval
options.explanation: Reversal would appear below the axis, not as an internal split of an above-axis region.

options.text: The velocity stayed constant throughout
options.explanation: A single rectangle would cover that; the split exists because the profile bends.

options.text: The graph was drawn inaccurately
options.explanation: The split is the lawful reading of a two-part profile, not a drawing fault.

check.stem: The worked journey's five areas are 350 m, 525 m, 75 m, 350 m and 875 m. Which arithmetic check confirms the total?

options.explanation: The five areas sum to 2175 m, the journey's total distance.
A product of five metre-values is dimensionally absurd for a distance.
Ratio-form combinations of areas are not part of the summation rule.
Subtracting component distances from the largest gives no journey quantity.

check.stem: The distance travelled between 70 s and 90 s of the worked journey is wanted. Which reading is correct?

options.text: The areas standing on the 70-90 s slice of the base, which are areas 3 and 4
options.explanation: An interval's distance is the area above its own slice of the time axis, here 75 + 350 = 425 m.

options.text: The whole graph's area divided by eight
options.explanation: There is no rule tying an interval to a fixed fraction of the total; slice the base instead.

options.text: The velocity values at 70 s and 90 s
options.explanation: Two heights are not a distance; the area between them over the interval is.

options.text: The area of the largest single shape on the graph
options.explanation: The largest shape may sit anywhere on the timeline; interval questions slice, not cherry-pick.

check.stem: A velocity-time line curves gently instead of staying straight. How is the distance still estimated?

options.text: Divide the curved region into many triangles and rectangles and add them
options.explanation: The same shape arithmetic, applied in small pieces, estimates the area under a curve.

options.text: Curved lines carry no area, so distance cannot be found
options.explanation: The area exists under any line; only the exact formulas need the straightness.

options.text: Read the final velocity and multiply by the total time
options.explanation: That rectangle uses only the endpoint and misses the shape of the whole profile.

options.text: Take the gradient of the curve and quote it
options.explanation: Gradient reads acceleration; the question asks for distance.

check.stem: State how each enclosed section's area is interpreted when a journey is split into pieces.
check.modelAnswer: Each enclosed section's area is the distance travelled during that section's own interval of time.

check.stem: Recall the five areas of the worked car journey in order and their total.
check.modelAnswer: The areas are 350 m, 525 m, 75 m, 350 m and 875 m, and their total distance is 2175 m.

check.stem: Explain why labelling each enclosed area before calculating protects the final answer.
check.modelAnswer: Labelling turns one long calculation into five short, checkable ones: if the total looks wrong, each labelled area can be tested against its own base and height. Without labels, a single slip is buried in the sum and cannot be traced, which is exactly where method marks are lost.

check.stem: A delivery van's graph shows a triangle (base 30 s, height 10 m/s), then a rectangle (base 40 s, height 10 m/s), then a triangle back to rest (base 50 s). Calculate the total distance of the delivery run.
check.modelAnswer: Triangle 1: ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m. Rectangle: 40 × 10 = 400 m. Triangle 2: ½ × 50 × 10 = 250 m. Total distance = 150 + 400 + 250 = 800 m.

glossary.definition: How far the object ends up from where it started; read from the enclosed area when the line stays above the axis.
A region fully bounded by the velocity-time line, the time axis and interval boundaries; each one is a distance.
The time-interval side of an enclosed shape, read along the horizontal axis.
The velocity side of an enclosed shape, read from the vertical axis.

workedExample.prompt: The velocity-time graph shows a car journey lasting 160 seconds. Calculate the total distance travelled by the car.
steps: Recall that the area under the line is the distance travelled, so the total area underneath must be found.
Identify the five enclosed areas under the line and label them 1 to 5.
Sum the five areas: total distance = 350 + 525 + 75 + 350 + 875 = 2175 m.
